script.opening: "For the last few days I’ve had this ache low down — sort of between my legs and in my back — it burns when I wee, I’m going all the time, and it even hurts when I ejaculate. I feel feverish and rough too. Is it just a water infection? Can I get some antibiotics?"

facts.text: Four days. A deep ache "behind my balls", in the perineum and low back. Worse sitting down. Testicles themselves not swollen or painful.
Burning on passing urine, going every hour, urgent, weaker stream than usual and a bit slow to start. "It comes, it just stings." No blood. Can still pass urine. Up 3 times at night.
Hot and cold sweats, shivery last night, aching all over. No thermometer. Not confused, not breathless, eating a little, drinking OK. No vomiting.
Married, one partner (wife, Claire) for 15 years; no other partners. No penile discharge or rash. Painful ejaculation since this started. Happy to be tested "if it helps".
Fit and well. Never had a urine infection. No medicines; occasional paracetamol (taken some this morning). No allergies. No recent catheter or procedures. Hasn’t had any antibiotics this year.

Self-employed electrician; "I can’t afford time off." Cycles to work most days (has stopped this week). Drinks 10–12 units a week, non-smoker. Lives with wife and two children; can get to the surgery this afternoon if needed.
Father had "prostate trouble" in his seventies. No cancers he knows of.

Uncomfortable, a bit embarrassed about the ejaculation pain — mention it in the opening but go quiet if the doctor doesn’t follow it up. You want quick antibiotics and are mildly impatient about coming in. Agree if the reason is explained. Be surprised the course is so long.

ice.ideas: "It’s a water infection. A few days of tablets and I’ll be fine."
ice.concerns: Only if asked: "The pain when I… finish — I wondered if that meant something serious, like cancer, or that I’d caught something." He needs to keep working.
ice.expectations: "A prescription sent to the chemist today, ideally without coming in."

cues: "It even hurts when I ejaculate" — embarrassing symptom and a pointer to the prostate.
"I feel feverish and rough" — needs an assessment for sepsis and observations.
"I can’t afford time off" — practical barrier to coming in and to a long course.

checkpoints.text: Recognises ACUTE PROSTATITIS (perineal/pelvic/back pain + LUTS + painful ejaculation + fever/systemic illness, tender prostate on gentle DRE at a same-day face-to-face assessment) as distinct from a simple "water infection"
Treats a UTI in a man as significant — sends a urine culture before antibiotics, considers an STI screen where relevant, and assesses the wider urinary-tract context

Assesses SEPSIS (fever, rigors, tachycardia, hypotension — NICE NG253, with observations face to face) and the ACUTE URINARY RETENTION red flag — recognising retention with prostatitis needs hospital referral (NICE NG110), where the catheter route (possibly suprapubic) is a specialist decision, not a routine attempt

Treats with an APPROPRIATE prostate-penetrating antibiotic (NICE NG110: ciprofloxacin/ofloxacin, or trimethoprim if a fluoroquinolone is not appropriate, weighing the MHRA January 2024 fluoroquinolone restriction and local advice) for a PROLONGED course (14 days, then review: stop or continue for a further 14 days), with analgesia — not a short cystitis course — and counsels fluoroquinolone cautions (MHRA) if one is used

Distinguishes acute prostatitis from CHRONIC prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (>3 months, often non-bacterial, multimodal management) and avoids checking PSA in acute infection (defer at least 6 weeks, UKHSA PCRMP)
Explains that this is more than a simple water infection and why a longer course is needed, addressing any embarrassment (ejaculatory pain) sensitively and checking understanding

Decides disposition — admit for IV antibiotics if septic/severe or retention, or refer if not improving within 48 hours (NICE NG110) — and considers urology referral if recurrent, abscess suspected, or retention

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent review for inability to pass urine (retention), worsening fever/rigors/sepsis, or no improvement within 48 hours; urine-culture-guided adjustment; review at 14 days; recheck and follow-up — adequate treatment, not a short course

worked.txt: "It’s related, but more than a simple water infection. The pain between your legs and in your back, the burning, going all the time, pain on ejaculating and the fever together point to an infection of the prostate gland — prostatitis. In men, urine infections are taken more seriously and need proper treatment."

"A couple of important checks: are you managing to pass urine okay, or struggling/unable to go? And how feverish — any shaking chills, feeling really unwell? … If you couldn’t pass urine or were septic, you’d need urgent hospital assessment. I also need to check your temperature, pulse and blood pressure and gently examine your prostate, which I can’t do on video, so I’d like to see you in person today."

"I’ll send a urine sample to identify the bug and guide treatment, and — I have to ask routinely — about sexual history, as some infections that cause this need a specific test. I won’t check a prostate (PSA) blood test now, as infection makes it misleading; if it’s needed, it waits at least 6 weeks."

"This needs an antibiotic that gets into the prostate — ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim; we’ll weigh which suits you, because ciprofloxacin has rare but serious side-effects — and crucially a longer course, 14 days, then I’ll review whether you need another 14, not the few days you’d have for simple cystitis, to clear it fully and stop it becoming chronic. I’ll add painkillers too."

"A note on that antibiotic — if we use ciprofloxacin, rarely it affects tendons, muscles, joints, nerves or mood, so stop it and contact us at the first sign of tendon pain or swelling, tingling or numbness, or changes in mood or thinking. If pelvic pain ever drags on for months without infection, that’s a different, longer-term condition we’d manage differently."

"Come back urgently — or A&E — if you can’t pass urine, get shaking chills/high fever, feel much worse, or aren’t starting to improve within 48 hours. I’ll check the urine result and review you at 14 days to make sure it’s clearing and decide whether to stop or continue for another 14. Don’t stop the antibiotics early even when you feel better."

f.learning: PERINEAL/pelvic/low back pain with LUTS (dysuria, frequency, urgency, hesitancy), PAINFUL EJACULATION and FEVER/systemic illness in a man is ACUTE PROSTATITIS — a bacterial infection of the prostate, with an exquisitely tender/boggy prostate on gentle DRE at a same-day face-to-face assessment (not possible by video) — not "just a water infection", and a urinary infection in a man is itself uncommon and significant. Send a urine culture before antibiotics (and consider an STI screen where sexual history is relevant, as chlamydia/gonorrhoea can cause prostatitis), and assess the wider urinary tract. Critically, assess for SEPSIS (high fever, rigors, tachycardia, hypotension — NICE NG253; may need admission/IV antibiotics) and the key red flag of ACUTE URINARY RETENTION, because NICE NG110 advises hospital referral for sepsis, retention or a suspected prostatic abscess, and in prostatitis the catheterisation route (urethral or suprapubic) is a specialist decision — so retention warrants urgent hospital/urology assessment rather than a routine attempt. Treat with an antibiotic that PENETRATES the prostate — NICE NG110: a FLUOROQUINOLONE (ciprofloxacin/ofloxacin), or trimethoprim if a fluoroquinolone is not appropriate, weighing the MHRA January 2024 restriction (fluoroquinolones only when other commonly recommended antibiotics are inappropriate) and local guidance/culture — for a PROLONGED course (14 days, then review and stop or continue for a further 14 days) to prevent chronic prostatitis/abscess, with analgesia, counselling fluoroquinolone cautions (tendon/aortic/neuropsychiatric/QT) and adjusting to culture; admit if septic/severe. Distinguish acute prostatitis from CHRONIC prostatitis/CHRONIC PELVIC PAIN SYNDROME (persistent pelvic/perineal pain and LUTS >3 months, often non-bacterial, managed multimodally). Do NOT measure PSA during acute infection (falsely elevated; defer at least 6 weeks, UKHSA PCRMP), and safety-net for retention, worsening sepsis or non-improvement within 48 hours (hospital referral, NICE NG110), with culture-guided follow-up and urology referral if recurrent, abscess suspected or retention. The hidden agenda is the wish for "antibiotics for a water infection"; recognise prostatitis as more than a simple UTI and treat it adequately, not as simple cystitis.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG110 (prostatitis, acute: antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update, fluoroquinolones (January 2024) · [3] NICE NG253 (suspected sepsis, 16 and over) · [4] NICE NG109 (lower UTI: antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [5] UKHSA Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme: advising well men about the PSA test · [6] EAU Chronic Pelvic Pain guideline (2025, international)
knowledge.summary: Perineal pain, urinary symptoms, painful ejaculation and fever in a man point to acute bacterial prostatitis, not simple cystitis. Assess for sepsis and retention the same day, send urine before antibiotics, and treat for 14 days with a review, not a 3-day course.

points.t: Acute prostatitis presents with perineal, pelvic, suprapubic or low back pain, dysuria, frequency, urgency or hesitancy, sometimes painful ejaculation, and fever or malaise. The prostate is typically very tender on a gentle rectal examination; prostatic massage is avoided in the acute phase (EAU, international). A video call cannot replace observations or examination, so arrange a same-day face-to-face assessment.

NICE NG110 [1]: send a midstream urine sample for culture before starting antibiotics. Ask a sexual history and offer chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing where there is any risk, because STIs can present similarly. NICE NG109 [4] is for lower UTI in men and uses a 7-day course; it does not cover prostatitis.

NICE NG110 [1]: refer to hospital if he has symptoms or signs of a more serious illness or condition such as sepsis, acute urinary retention or a prostatic abscess. Assess sepsis risk with NICE NG253 [3] (heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen saturation, mental state). Retention in acute prostatitis is a hospital problem; the route of catheterisation is a specialist decision.

NICE NG110 [1] first choices: ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or ofloxacin 200 mg twice daily for 14 days; if a fluoroquinolone is not appropriate, trimethoprim 200 mg twice daily for 14 days. MHRA Drug Safety Update (January 2024) [2]: systemic fluoroquinolones must only be used when other commonly recommended antibiotics are inappropriate. Weigh this for the individual man, take local microbiology advice where available, record the reason for the choice, and adjust to culture.

If a fluoroquinolone is used, MHRA [2] advice is to tell him to stop and seek help at the first sign of tendon pain or swelling, muscle or joint pain, numbness or tingling, or changes in mood or thinking; extra caution with corticosteroids, age over 60 and renal impairment.

NICE NG110 [1]: symptoms should improve within 48 hours; refer to hospital if they do not, or if he gets worse at any time. At 14 days, review and either stop or continue for a further 14 days if needed. Analgesia: paracetamol, with or without a low-dose weak opioid, or ibuprofen.
UKHSA PCRMP [5]: do not measure PSA during an active urinary infection; defer for at least 6 weeks. A PSA taken now would be falsely raised and could trigger an unnecessary referral.

Chronic prostatitis or chronic pelvic pain syndrome means pelvic or perineal pain for at least 3 of the previous 6 months, usually without fever. It is managed differently (EAU 2025 [6], international: alpha-blocker if under 1 year, pain-focused and psychological approaches). MHRA advises against fluoroquinolones for non-bacterial chronic prostatitis.

dg.d: Private setting checked; open question; let him describe the pain, urinary symptoms and fever fully.
The wish for a quick fix; embarrassment about ejaculatory pain; sexual history asked without judgement.
Same-day face-to-face: observations, abdominal and gentle prostate examination with chaperone; MSU before antibiotics; STI NAAT; no PSA.
Acute prostatitis vs lower UTI, urethritis or STI, epididymo-orchitis, chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
Screened retention, sepsis (NG253 features) and haematuria; recognised that hospital referral applies to sepsis, retention or abscess.
Acute bacterial prostatitis, more than simple cystitis.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Allergies and medicines checked; the wish to avoid a visit acknowledged; plan for chronic symptoms if they follow.
A&E for retention or sepsis signs; ring if not improving by 48 hours; results call; review at 14 days to stop or extend.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “feverish and rough” and “hurts when I ejaculate” and linked both to prostatitis.
Idea (a simple water infection), concern (painful ejaculation meaning something serious), expectation (a few days of tablets).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Beckett, I’m Dr Shah. Can you hear and see me clearly, and are you somewhere you can talk privately? … Good. What’s been going on?
model.why: Checks connection and privacy before an intimate history

model.text: For the last few days I’ve had this ache low down, sort of between my legs and in my back. It burns when I wee, I’m going all the time, and it even hurts when I ejaculate. I feel feverish and rough too. Is it just a water infection? Can I get some antibiotics?

Thank you for being so clear, I know some of that isn’t easy to say. You sound quite unwell with it. I’ll definitely help you get treated. Can I ask some questions first, so we get the right treatment for the right length of time?
model.why: Acknowledges embarrassment and illness; signposts the plan

model.text: Yes, fine.
First, the most important one: are you able to pass urine at the moment, or are you straining, or feel you can’t empty?
I can go. It’s slow and it stings, but it comes.
And the fever: have you had shaking chills, or felt faint, confused or breathless? Have you been able to check your temperature?
I’ve felt hot and cold. I haven’t got a thermometer. I’m not confused or anything.
Any blood in the urine, pain in your testicles or scrotum, or discharge from the penis?
No blood, no discharge. The ache is behind, not in my testicles.
Have you had anything like this before, or any pelvic pain lasting months?
No, this came on over a few days.
I ask everyone this with these symptoms, because some infections caught through sex look very similar: is there any chance of a sexually transmitted infection?
model.why: Non-judgemental sexual history to decide on STI testing

model.text: I don’t think so, but test me if it helps.
Any medical problems, regular medicines or allergies to antibiotics?
model.why: Checks allergies and interactions before prescribing

model.text: No, nothing.
You mentioned a water infection. What were you expecting today?
A few days of tablets. I just want it sorted quickly.
That makes sense. Is anything else worrying you about it, for example the pain when you ejaculate?
A bit. I didn’t know if that meant something serious.

Here’s what I think. The pain between your legs and in your back, the burning, going often, pain on ejaculating and the fever all fit an infection of the prostate gland, called acute prostatitis. It explains the ejaculation pain, so that isn’t a separate worry. It’s more than a simple water infection, and it needs a longer course of treatment than cystitis would.
model.why: Clear working diagnosis linked to his symptoms and concern

model.text: Longer? How long?
Usually two weeks, and then we review. The prostate is harder for antibiotics to reach, and stopping early risks it coming back or grumbling on.

Because you have a fever I need to check you properly today, not just over video. I’d like you to come in this afternoon so we can check your temperature, pulse and blood pressure, feel your tummy, and gently examine the prostate with a chaperone offered. Please bring a urine sample so we can send it to the lab before you start antibiotics.
model.why: Same-day face-to-face: observations, examination, MSU before antibiotics

model.text: Can you not just send the prescription?

I understand you wanted to avoid a trip in. The honest reason is that if your observations show the infection is spreading into your blood, you’d need hospital treatment through a drip, and I can’t tell that on a screen. If everything is stable, you’ll go home with tablets today.
model.why: Negotiates the visit with a transparent reason

model.text: Okay, I can get there.

For the antibiotic, there are two main options. One group, like ciprofloxacin, gets into the prostate well, but the medicines regulator now asks us to use it only when other antibiotics aren’t suitable, because of rare but serious side effects on tendons, nerves and mood. The other option is trimethoprim. I’ll choose with you when I’ve seen you and the urine test, and we can switch if the lab result points elsewhere.
model.why: NG110 options with MHRA January 2024 restriction; culture-guided

model.text: I didn’t know antibiotics could do that.

It’s uncommon, and I’ll tell you exactly what to watch for if you do need it. Paracetamol or ibuprofen will help the pain. I’ll also send the test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. One thing I won’t do now is a PSA prostate blood test: infection pushes it up and it would give a misleading result.
model.why: Analgesia, STI test, avoids PSA in acute infection

model.text: Two things mean go straight to A&E: if you can’t pass urine at all, or you get shaking, feel faint, confused or much more unwell. You should feel better within two days of starting antibiotics. If not, ring us that day, as that would also mean hospital. Can you tell me back the plan?
model.why: Specific safety-net: retention, sepsis, no improvement at 48 hours

model.text: Come in this afternoon with a wee sample. Two weeks of tablets. A&E if I can’t wee or get really poorly, call if I’m not better in two days.

Exactly. I’ll ring you with the urine result and see you again at two weeks to decide whether to stop or carry on. If the pain were to carry on for months afterwards, that’s a different condition we’d manage differently, so do come back.
model.why: Results, 14-day review, chronic pelvic pain signposted

model.text: Thanks, doctor. Glad I didn’t just get three days of tablets.

social.t: Wanting tablets without a visit is common. A same-day visit and a clear two-week plan are easier to accept when the reason is explained.
Ejaculatory pain and perineal symptoms are often under-reported. Asking gently and linking them to the diagnosis relieves an unspoken worry.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone for the rectal examination and record the offer and his response.

GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. A febrile man with possible prostatitis needs observations first.

professional.t: Follow NICE NG110 for choice and duration; apply the MHRA January 2024 fluoroquinolone restriction and record why a fluoroquinolone was or was not used.
If he works and is unfit to, he can self-certify for the first 7 days; a fit note can be issued after that if needed.

community.t: Local sexual health clinics offer confidential STI testing and partner notification if a test is positive.

redFlags: Unable to pass urine or a painful distended bladder (acute retention)
Rigors, fainting, confusion, breathlessness or very high fever (possible sepsis)
Not improving 48 hours after starting antibiotics
psychosocial: The wish for a quick prescription without a visit
Sexual health context, asked routinely and without judgement
ice: Concern: whether painful ejaculation means something serious
Expectation: a few days of antibiotics without having to come in

playbook.diagnosis: “The pain between your legs and in your back, the burning, going often, pain on ejaculating and the fever point to an infection of the prostate gland, called acute prostatitis. It’s more than a simple water infection.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The prostate is a small gland tucked under the bladder, like a sponge around the water pipe. When it’s infected it swells and aches, and antibiotics find it harder to soak into, which is why the course is longer.”

management.reflectIce: “You expected a few days of tablets like a water infection. This is a bit different, so I want to check you today and give you a proper two-week course. The pain when you ejaculate is part of the same infection.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge that he wanted to avoid a visit; offer a same-day slot that suits him; fit note if needed; address the embarrassment by explaining the symptom.
sharedPlan: Same-day face-to-face: observations with NG253 risk assessment, abdominal and gentle prostate examination (chaperone offered)
MSU for culture before antibiotics; chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT

NICE NG110 14-day course: ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin, or trimethoprim if a fluoroquinolone is not appropriate; fluoroquinolone only when other options are inappropriate (MHRA January 2024), with counselling
Paracetamol with or without low-dose weak opioid, or ibuprofen
No PSA now; defer at least 6 weeks if indicated later
safetyNet: A&E if unable to pass urine, rigors, faintness, confusion or rapid worsening
Ring the same day if not improving 48 hours after starting antibiotics
Results call; review at 14 days to stop or continue a further 14 days
Return if pelvic pain persists for months after the infection

pitfalls.intro: The trap is agreeing to his framing. A febrile man with perineal pain is not a three-day cystitis prescription over video. Marks sit in the red-flag screen, the same-day assessment and an evidence-based course.

items.why: NG110 treats acute prostatitis for 14 days with review; a short course risks relapse or chronic infection.
items.fix: “This needs a two-week course and a review.”

items.fail: Never asking whether he can pass urine or about rigors and faintness.
items.why: Retention and sepsis are the reasons for hospital referral in NG110 and must be screened.
items.fix: Ask retention first, then sepsis features, out loud.

items.fail: Prescribing remotely with no observations or urine culture.
items.why: A fever needs NG253 observations; NG110 asks for an MSU before antibiotics.
items.fix: Arrange a same-day face-to-face and ask him to bring urine.

items.fail: Choosing ciprofloxacin reflexively with no counselling.
items.why: MHRA January 2024: fluoroquinolones only when other recommended antibiotics are inappropriate; patients must know what to report.
items.fix: Discuss both NG110 options, record the reason, and counsel on tendon, nerve and mood effects if used.

items.fail: Ignoring the painful ejaculation because it is awkward.
items.why: It is his hidden worry and part of the diagnosis.
items.fix: “That pain is part of the same prostate infection, not a separate problem.”

items.why: Vague safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: A&E for retention or sepsis signs; ring if not better by 48 hours; review at 14 days.

Retention, sepsis features, haematuria, testicular pain, discharge, chronic pain, sexual history, allergies.
His “water infection” model, the ejaculatory pain worry, and his wish for quick tablets.

wordPics.pass: Recognises acute prostatitis, arranges same-day observations and urine culture, prescribes a 14-day course per NG110, screens retention and sepsis, and tells him when to go to A&E.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains why video is not enough and negotiates the visit; weighs NG110 first choices against the MHRA January 2024 fluoroquinolone restriction and counsels accordingly; links the ejaculatory pain to the diagnosis to relieve his worry; defers PSA with a reason; teach-back; 48-hour and 14-day review points.

avoid.instead: “This fits an infection of the prostate. It needs a check today and a two-week course.”
avoid.why: Undertreats a prostatic infection and skips the sepsis and retention assessment.

Any medical problems, regular medicines or allergies to antibiotics?
SCA_MODELS.why: Checks allergies and interactions before prescribing

SCA_MODELS.text: No, nothing.
You mentioned a water infection. What were you expecting today?
A few days of tablets. I just want it sorted quickly.
That makes sense. Is anything else worrying you about it, for example the pain when you ejaculate?
A bit. I didn’t know if that meant something serious.

Here’s what I think. The pain between your legs and in your back, the burning, going often, pain on ejaculating and the fever all fit an infection of the prostate gland, called acute prostatitis. It explains the ejaculation pain, so that isn’t a separate worry. It’s more than a simple water infection, and it needs a longer course of treatment than cystitis would.
SCA_MODELS.why: Clear working diagnosis linked to his symptoms and concern

SCA_MODELS.text: Longer? How long?
Usually two weeks, and then we review. The prostate is harder for antibiotics to reach, and stopping early risks it coming back or grumbling on.

Because you have a fever I need to check you properly today, not just over video. I’d like you to come in this afternoon so we can check your temperature, pulse and blood pressure, feel your tummy, and gently examine the prostate with a chaperone offered. Please bring a urine sample so we can send it to the lab before you start antibiotics.
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day face-to-face: observations, examination, MSU before antibiotics

SCA_MODELS.text: Can you not just send the prescription?

I understand you wanted to avoid a trip in. The honest reason is that if your observations show the infection is spreading into your blood, you’d need hospital treatment through a drip, and I can’t tell that on a screen. If everything is stable, you’ll go home with tablets today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Negotiates the visit with a transparent reason

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay, I can get there.

For the antibiotic, there are two main options. One group, like ciprofloxacin, gets into the prostate well, but the medicines regulator now asks us to use it only when other antibiotics aren’t suitable, because of rare but serious side effects on tendons, nerves and mood. The other option is trimethoprim. I’ll choose with you when I’ve seen you and the urine test, and we can switch if the lab result points elsewhere.
SCA_MODELS.why: NG110 options with MHRA January 2024 restriction; culture-guided

SCA_MODELS.text: I didn’t know antibiotics could do that.

It’s uncommon, and I’ll tell you exactly what to watch for if you do need it. Paracetamol or ibuprofen will help the pain. I’ll also send the test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. One thing I won’t do now is a PSA prostate blood test: infection pushes it up and it would give a misleading result.
SCA_MODELS.why: Analgesia, STI test, avoids PSA in acute infection

SCA_MODELS.text: Two things mean go straight to A&E: if you can’t pass urine at all, or you get shaking, feel faint, confused or much more unwell. You should feel better within two days of starting antibiotics. If not, ring us that day, as that would also mean hospital. Can you tell me back the plan?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net: retention, sepsis, no improvement at 48 hours

SCA_MODELS.text: Come in this afternoon with a wee sample. Two weeks of tablets. A&E if I can’t wee or get really poorly, call if I’m not better in two days.

Exactly. I’ll ring you with the urine result and see you again at two weeks to decide whether to stop or carry on. If the pain were to carry on for months afterwards, that’s a different condition we’d manage differently, so do come back.
SCA_MODELS.why: Results, 14-day review, chronic pelvic pain signposted

SCA_MODELS.text: Thanks, doctor. Glad I didn’t just get three days of tablets.

SCA_STEM.name: Owen Beckett
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations for urinary symptoms.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: several days of pain “down below”, burning on passing urine and feeling feverish; asking for antibiotics for a water infection.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG110 (prostatitis, acute: antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update, fluoroquinolones (January 2024) · [3] NICE NG253 (suspected sepsis, 16 and over) · [4] NICE NG109 (lower UTI: antimicrobial prescribing, 2018) · [5] UKHSA Prostate Cancer Risk Management Programme: advising well men about the PSA test · [6] EAU Chronic Pelvic Pain guideline (2025, international)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Perineal pain, urinary symptoms, painful ejaculation and fever in a man point to acute bacterial prostatitis, not simple cystitis. Assess for sepsis and retention the same day, send urine before antibiotics, and treat for 14 days with a review, not a 3-day course.

points.t: Acute prostatitis presents with perineal, pelvic, suprapubic or low back pain, dysuria, frequency, urgency or hesitancy, sometimes painful ejaculation, and fever or malaise. The prostate is typically very tender on a gentle rectal examination; prostatic massage is avoided in the acute phase (EAU, international). A video call cannot replace observations or examination, so arrange a same-day face-to-face assessment.

NICE NG110 [1]: send a midstream urine sample for culture before starting antibiotics. Ask a sexual history and offer chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing where there is any risk, because STIs can present similarly. NICE NG109 [4] is for lower UTI in men and uses a 7-day course; it does not cover prostatitis.

NICE NG110 [1]: refer to hospital if he has symptoms or signs of a more serious illness or condition such as sepsis, acute urinary retention or a prostatic abscess. Assess sepsis risk with NICE NG253 [3] (heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen saturation, mental state). Retention in acute prostatitis is a hospital problem; the route of catheterisation is a specialist decision.

NICE NG110 [1] first choices: ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or ofloxacin 200 mg twice daily for 14 days; if a fluoroquinolone is not appropriate, trimethoprim 200 mg twice daily for 14 days. MHRA Drug Safety Update (January 2024) [2]: systemic fluoroquinolones must only be used when other commonly recommended antibiotics are inappropriate. Weigh this for the individual man, take local microbiology advice where available, record the reason for the choice, and adjust to culture.

If a fluoroquinolone is used, MHRA [2] advice is to tell him to stop and seek help at the first sign of tendon pain or swelling, muscle or joint pain, numbness or tingling, or changes in mood or thinking; extra caution with corticosteroids, age over 60 and renal impairment.

NICE NG110 [1]: symptoms should improve within 48 hours; refer to hospital if they do not, or if he gets worse at any time. At 14 days, review and either stop or continue for a further 14 days if needed. Analgesia: paracetamol, with or without a low-dose weak opioid, or ibuprofen.
UKHSA PCRMP [5]: do not measure PSA during an active urinary infection; defer for at least 6 weeks. A PSA taken now would be falsely raised and could trigger an unnecessary referral.

Chronic prostatitis or chronic pelvic pain syndrome means pelvic or perineal pain for at least 3 of the previous 6 months, usually without fever. It is managed differently (EAU 2025 [6], international: alpha-blocker if under 1 year, pain-focused and psychological approaches). MHRA advises against fluoroquinolones for non-bacterial chronic prostatitis.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Private setting checked; open question; let him describe the pain, urinary symptoms and fever fully.
The wish for a quick fix; embarrassment about ejaculatory pain; sexual history asked without judgement.
Picked up “feverish and rough” and “hurts when I ejaculate” and linked both to prostatitis.
Idea (a simple water infection), concern (painful ejaculation meaning something serious), expectation (a few days of tablets).
Same-day face-to-face: observations, abdominal and gentle prostate examination with chaperone; MSU before antibiotics; STI NAAT; no PSA.
Acute prostatitis vs lower UTI, urethritis or STI, epididymo-orchitis, chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
Screened retention, sepsis (NG253 features) and haematuria; recognised that hospital referral applies to sepsis, retention or abscess.
Acute bacterial prostatitis, more than simple cystitis.
14-day course per NG110; fluoroquinolone only if other options inappropriate (MHRA January 2024), counselling if used; analgesia; culture-guided.
Allergies and medicines checked; the wish to avoid a visit acknowledged; plan for chronic symptoms if they follow.
A&E for retention or sepsis signs; ring if not improving by 48 hours; results call; review at 14 days to stop or extend.

social.t: Wanting tablets without a visit is common. A same-day visit and a clear two-week plan are easier to accept when the reason is explained.
Ejaculatory pain and perineal symptoms are often under-reported. Asking gently and linking them to the diagnosis relieves an unspoken worry.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone for the rectal examination and record the offer and his response.

GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. A febrile man with possible prostatitis needs observations first.

professional.t: Follow NICE NG110 for choice and duration; apply the MHRA January 2024 fluoroquinolone restriction and record why a fluoroquinolone was or was not used.
If he works and is unfit to, he can self-certify for the first 7 days; a fit note can be issued after that if needed.

community.t: Local sexual health clinics offer confidential STI testing and partner notification if a test is positive.

redFlags: Unable to pass urine or a painful distended bladder (acute retention)
Rigors, fainting, confusion, breathlessness or very high fever (possible sepsis)
Not improving 48 hours after starting antibiotics
psychosocial: The wish for a quick prescription without a visit
Sexual health context, asked routinely and without judgement
ice: Concern: whether painful ejaculation means something serious
Expectation: a few days of antibiotics without having to come in

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The pain between your legs and in your back, the burning, going often, pain on ejaculating and the fever point to an infection of the prostate gland, called acute prostatitis. It’s more than a simple water infection.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The prostate is a small gland tucked under the bladder, like a sponge around the water pipe. When it’s infected it swells and aches, and antibiotics find it harder to soak into, which is why the course is longer.”

management.reflectIce: “You expected a few days of tablets like a water infection. This is a bit different, so I want to check you today and give you a proper two-week course. The pain when you ejaculate is part of the same infection.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge that he wanted to avoid a visit; offer a same-day slot that suits him; fit note if needed; address the embarrassment by explaining the symptom.
sharedPlan: Same-day face-to-face: observations with NG253 risk assessment, abdominal and gentle prostate examination (chaperone offered)
MSU for culture before antibiotics; chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT

NICE NG110 14-day course: ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin, or trimethoprim if a fluoroquinolone is not appropriate; fluoroquinolone only when other options are inappropriate (MHRA January 2024), with counselling
Paracetamol with or without low-dose weak opioid, or ibuprofen
No PSA now; defer at least 6 weeks if indicated later
safetyNet: A&E if unable to pass urine, rigors, faintness, confusion or rapid worsening
Ring the same day if not improving 48 hours after starting antibiotics
Results call; review at 14 days to stop or continue a further 14 days
Return if pelvic pain persists for months after the infection

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is agreeing to his framing. A febrile man with perineal pain is not a three-day cystitis prescription over video. Marks sit in the red-flag screen, the same-day assessment and an evidence-based course.

items.why: NG110 treats acute prostatitis for 14 days with review; a short course risks relapse or chronic infection.
items.fix: “This needs a two-week course and a review.”

items.fail: Never asking whether he can pass urine or about rigors and faintness.
items.why: Retention and sepsis are the reasons for hospital referral in NG110 and must be screened.
items.fix: Ask retention first, then sepsis features, out loud.

items.fail: Prescribing remotely with no observations or urine culture.
items.why: A fever needs NG253 observations; NG110 asks for an MSU before antibiotics.
items.fix: Arrange a same-day face-to-face and ask him to bring urine.

items.fail: Choosing ciprofloxacin reflexively with no counselling.
items.why: MHRA January 2024: fluoroquinolones only when other recommended antibiotics are inappropriate; patients must know what to report.
items.fix: Discuss both NG110 options, record the reason, and counsel on tendon, nerve and mood effects if used.

items.fail: Ignoring the painful ejaculation because it is awkward.
items.why: It is his hidden worry and part of the diagnosis.
items.fix: “That pain is part of the same prostate infection, not a separate problem.”

items.why: Vague safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: A&E for retention or sepsis signs; ring if not better by 48 hours; review at 14 days.
